Task 1 – Analysis. Text A: opening of "Dulce et Decorum Est" by Wilfred Owen (written 1917, published 1920).

Bent double, like old beggars under sacks,
Knock-kneed, coughing like hags, we cursed through sludge,
Till on the haunting flares we turned our backs,
And towards our distant rest began to trudge.
Men marched asleep. Many had lost their boots,
But limped on, blood-shod. All went lame; all blind;

How does Owen use imagery to present the reality of war in this opening?
Refer closely to the text, using short quotations, and explain the effects of the writer's choices.
items.answer: Owen presents soldiers not as heroes but as broken men: the similes "like old beggars under sacks" and "coughing like hags" age and degrade them, and "blood-shod" replaces boots with blood. Hyperbole ("All went lame; all blind") stresses total exhaustion, and the heavy rhythm with caesuras mimics their trudge. Written from a soldier's perspective, the imagery protests against the heroic language of propaganda.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Owen presents soldiers not as heroes but as broken men: the similes "like old beggars under sacks" and "coughing like hags" age and degrade them, and "blood-shod" replaces boots with blood. Hyperbole ("All went lame; all blind") stresses total exhaustion, and the heavy rhythm with caesuras mimics their trudge. Written from a soldier's perspective, the imagery protests against the heroic language of propaganda. Criterion A (scaled to 5): 5 perceptive analysis of several choices with precise evidence; 3-4 substantial; 2 adequate; 1 limited.

Task 1 – Analysis. Text B: parody advertisement from a student magazine.

[Image: a glossy bottle labelled PERFECT™ on a pink background with sparkles.]
TIRED OF BEING YOURSELF?
Introducing PERFECT™ – the filter you can drink!
✓ Removes freckles, opinions and personality
✓ Makes you look exactly like everyone else on your feed
✓ Side effects may include: loss of self, endless scrolling, and spending all your money
Because you're worth nothing... until you're PERFECT™.

How does the parody use the conventions of advertising to criticise beauty culture?
Refer closely to the text, using short quotations, and explain the effects of the writer's choices.
items.answer: The parody copies real advertising conventions – a glossy product shot, a problem question, ticked benefits, a trademark and a slogan – so readers recognise the genre. Exaggeration exposes the hidden message: the ticked list moves from freckles to "opinions and personality", and the side effects list loss of self. The twisted slogan "Because you're worth nothing... until you're PERFECT™" alludes to real cosmetic slogans and reveals how they sell insecurity.

Task 1 – Comparative analysis. Text A: report of a climate protest (Report A, from a national newspaper).

STUDENTS BRING CITY TO STANDSTILL
Thousands of school pupils skipped lessons on Friday to block the main bridge into the city, causing traffic delays of up to two hours.
Police said three people were arrested for public disorder.
"My son should be in maths, not in the road," said commuter Peter Hale.
Organisers claimed 12,000 attended, though police estimated 5,000.

Text B: report of a climate protest (Report B, from a youth news website).

12,000 YOUNG PEOPLE DEMAND CLIMATE ACTION
Up to 12,000 students marched peacefully across the main bridge on Friday, calling on the government to meet its emissions targets.
"We're missing one day of school. Our future is missing a plan," said organiser Amara Diallo, 16.
Scientists from the city university joined the march.
Police reported three arrests.

Compare how the two reports represent the same protest. Write a comparative response that analyses both texts, using evidence and comparative connectives.
items.answer: Both report the same basic facts (a march on the main bridge on Friday, three arrests), but they represent it differently. Report A's headline ("BRING CITY TO STANDSTILL") and focus on skipped lessons, traffic and a critical commuter frame the students as disruptive; it ends with the lower police estimate. Report B's headline uses the organisers' figure and the cause ("DEMAND CLIMATE ACTION"), stresses "peacefully", quotes a young organiser and mentions scientists, placing the arrests last. Selection, order, quotation and numbers create bias in both.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Both report the same basic facts (a march on the main bridge on Friday, three arrests), but they represent it differently. Report A's headline ("BRING CITY TO STANDSTILL") and focus on skipped lessons, traffic and a critical commuter frame the students as disruptive; it ends with the lower police estimate. Report B's headline uses the organisers' figure and the cause ("DEMAND CLIMATE ACTION"), stresses "peacefully", quotes a young organiser and mentions scientists, placing the arrests last. Selection, order, quotation and numbers create bias in both. MYP criteria (each 0-8, scaled to this item). A Analysing: explains content, context, language, structure, technique and style and their effects; justifies opinions with examples and explanation, using terminology. B Organising: a clear, logical structure suited to the task; ideas linked with purpose; referencing conventions. C Producing text: insight, imagination and personal engagement; deliberate stylistic choices; relevant detail and examples. D Using language: varied, accurate vocabulary, sentence structures and forms of expression; appropriate register and style; accurate grammar, spelling and punctuation. 7-8 perceptive/excellent; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate; 1-2 limited. (A 8, B 4, D 8 scaled to 20.)

Task 1 – Analysis. Text A: extract from Act 3 Scene 1 of Romeo and Juliet by William Shakespeare.

(TYBALT, under ROMEO's arm, stabs MERCUTIO, and flies with his followers.)
MERCUTIO: I am hurt.
A plague o' both your houses! I am sped.
ROMEO: Courage, man; the hurt cannot be much.
MERCUTIO: No, 'tis not so deep as a well, nor so wide as a church-door; but 'tis enough, 'twill serve: ask for me to-morrow, and you shall find me a grave man.

How does Shakespeare make Mercutio's death a turning point in the play?
Refer closely to the text, using short quotations, and explain the effects of the writer's choices.
items.answer: The stage direction shows Tybalt striking "under Romeo's arm", so Romeo's attempt at peace causes the death. Mercutio's curse "A plague o' both your houses!" blames both families and foreshadows tragedy. His dying pun ("a grave man") keeps his wit to the end, making the loss poignant. Romeo's ironic reassurance increases tension, and the death drives Romeo to revenge, turning the play from romance to tragedy.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: The stage direction shows Tybalt striking "under Romeo's arm", so Romeo's attempt at peace causes the death. Mercutio's curse "A plague o' both your houses!" blames both families and foreshadows tragedy. His dying pun ("a grave man") keeps his wit to the end, making the loss poignant. Romeo's ironic reassurance increases tension, and the death drives Romeo to revenge, turning the play from romance to tragedy. Criterion A (scaled to 5): 5 perceptive analysis of several choices with precise evidence; 3-4 substantial; 2 adequate; 1 limited.

Task 1 – Analysis. Text B: film review on a student film blog.

Tidewater (12A) ★★★★☆
Director Ana Moreno's debut follows two sisters in a Chilean fishing village as the sea swallows their town, house by house.
The cinematography is breathtaking: long, wide shots of grey water make the people look painfully small, while handheld close-ups during the storm put you right in the boat.
The script stumbles in the middle – a romance subplot goes nowhere – but the final ten minutes, almost silent, left our whole row in tears.
Verdict: a quiet film about a loud problem. Bring tissues.

How does the reviewer make the review informative and persuasive?
Refer closely to the text, using short quotations, and explain the effects of the writer's choices.
items.answer: The star rating and verdict give a quick judgement, and the spoiler-free summary informs. Technical vocabulary (wide shots, handheld close-ups) explains how the film creates effects and builds the reviewer's credibility. Honest criticism of the subplot adds balance, while personal response ("our whole row in tears") and the antithetical verdict persuade readers to watch.

Task 1 – Comparative analysis. Text A: advertisement for running shoes, printed in a teen sports magazine.

[Image: a girl sprints up concrete steps at dawn; the city below is still asleep.]
THEY SAID TOO YOUNG. THEY SAID TOO SMALL. THEY SAID TOO LATE.
She said: watch me.
STRIDE X – featherlight foam, grip that never quits.
Your city. Your rules. Your run.
#RunYourWay  |  Available now in 12 colours.

Text B: interview from a teen magazine with a young chef in Lima.

At 16, Valentina Rojas runs a weekend food stall in Lima that sells out in two hours. We asked her how.
Q: Where did you learn to cook?
A: My abuela's kitchen. She never measured anything. She'd say, 'Cook until it smells like home.'
Q: What's the hardest part?
A: Waking up at 4 a.m. to buy fish. And being taken seriously. People ask where my parents are.
Q: Advice for other teens?
A: Start small. Burn things. Try again.

Compare how the two texts present young people's determination to succeed. Write a comparative response that analyses both texts, using evidence and comparative connectives.
items.answer: Text A (advert) dramatises determination through anaphora ("THEY SAID TOO YOUNG...") and a defiant reply, using it to sell shoes; Text B (interview) lets a real young chef describe hardships (4 a.m. starts, not being taken seriously) and ends with the tricolon "Start small. Burn things. Try again." Both show young people proving doubters wrong. Difference: the advert's determination is an image constructed for profit; the interview's is grounded in specific detail and modest humour, making it more convincing.

items.stem:
Task 1 – Analysis. Text A: poem by a student poet, "My Grandmother's Hands".

Her hands are maps of seventy years,
rivers of blue beneath brown paper skin.
They knead the dough like they are
pressing out the war, the boat, the cold.
Flour rises like snow in reverse.
When she holds mine, I feel the journey –
every border folded into her palms.

How does the poet use imagery to present the grandmother and her past?
Refer closely to the text, using short quotations, and explain the effects of the writer's choices.
items.answer: The extended map metaphor ("maps of seventy years", "every border folded into her palms") presents her hands as a record of a journey across borders. The simile of kneading out "the war, the boat, the cold" shows her quietly working through trauma, while "Flour rises like snow in reverse" softens the past into warmth. The speaker's touch ("When she holds mine") passes the history on.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: The extended map metaphor ("maps of seventy years", "every border folded into her palms") presents her hands as a record of a journey across borders. The simile of kneading out "the war, the boat, the cold" shows her quietly working through trauma, while "Flour rises like snow in reverse" softens the past into warmth. The speaker's touch ("When she holds mine") passes the history on. Criterion A (scaled to 5): 5 perceptive analysis of several choices with precise evidence; 3-4 substantial; 2 adequate; 1 limited.

Task 1 – Analysis. Text B: speech by a student council president to her school assembly in Toronto.

Good morning, everyone. Raise your hand if you checked your phone before breakfast today. (Pause.) Me too.
We are the most connected generation in history – and, according to our own school survey, 62 per cent of us say we feel lonely every week. Connected, but alone.
I'm not asking you to throw your phone in the lake. I'm asking for one hour. One lunchtime a week, phones in our bags, eyes on each other.
Let's try it. Let's talk. Let's remember what our friends' faces look like when they laugh.

How does the speaker persuade her audience to try a phone-free lunchtime?
Refer closely to the text, using short quotations, and explain the effects of the writer's choices.
items.answer: The speaker builds trust before persuading: the opening show of hands and "Me too" make the habit shared, not shameful (ethos). The school statistic and the paradox "Connected, but alone" give logical and emotional weight. The humorous concession shrinks the request to "one hour", and the anaphoric "Let's..." ending turns agreement into collective action, closing on the emotive image of friends laughing.

Task 1 – Comparative analysis. Text A: travel blog post by a 15-year-old visiting Iceland.

Day 4: I Stood Next to a Volcano (and Lived)
Posted by @nadia_explores
OK, so technically the eruption at Fagradalsfjall had stopped. But the ground was still breathing. Steam curled out of black rock like the earth was exhaling after a long run.
Our guide, Sigga, said the lava field was younger than me. I didn't know rocks could be younger than me!!
My boots smelled of sulphur (rotten eggs, basically) for two days. Worth it.
Drop a 🌋 in the comments if Iceland is on your list!

Text B: diary entry by a 13-year-old on a school expedition in the Scottish Highlands.

Wednesday 14 May
Today was the WORST and maybe the BEST day of my life.
We walked 18 km in the rain. My boots filled with water like two buckets. Leo's map blew into a loch. We argued for twenty minutes about which way was north.
Then the clouds split open and there it was: the whole valley, gold and green, with a rainbow sitting on it like a crown.
Nobody said anything for ages. Even Leo stopped complaining.
Tomorrow: 22 km. Help.

Compare how the two writers present an encounter with the natural world. Write a comparative response that analyses both texts, using evidence and comparative connectives.
items.answer: Both are first-person, informal, humorous accounts of a challenging outdoor experience. Text A (blog) addresses a public audience with emoji, a handle and a comment invitation, and uses personification ("the ground was still breathing") to make the volcano alive. Text B (private diary) moves from comic misery ("like two buckets") to awe at the valley ("a rainbow ... like a crown"). Difference: the blog performs for followers; the diary records honest private feelings, including a moment of silent wonder.

items.markingKey: Indicative content (Image 1 example): a missed bus that changes a day, a forgotten bag that holds a secret, or a moment of rebellion; a first-person narrator; structure: the missed bus – opening the bag – an unexpected consequence; techniques such as pathetic fallacy, a twist, short paragraphs. Any image and form may be chosen; the piece should go beyond literal description of the image. Mark mainly against criterion C (Producing text) and D (Using language), with B (Organising). 7-8 equivalent: imaginative, insightful response with deliberate stylistic choices for effect, a controlled structure and varied, precise, accurate language; 5-6: substantial engagement and mostly effective choices; 3-4: adequate but uneven; 1-2: limited, with frequent errors that obscure meaning.
